Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant combination of class imbalance, catastrophic forgetting, and background shift in continual semantic segmentation. Combining retained class prototypes with learned membership assignments for multiple unknown clusters is potentially useful.

The empirical evaluation is substantial, covering ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and Cityscapes with multiple incremental schedules and CNN/transformer architectures. Within the DeepLab-V3 comparisons, FALCON improves over FairCL from 34.7 to 36.4 mIoU on ADE20K 100-10, from 67.61 to 69.83 on VOC 15-1, and from 49.22 to 55.24 on Cityscapes 1-1.

The ablations provide positive evidence beyond aggregate benchmark performance. In Table 1, the proposed loss increases minority-class mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8 on ADE20K 100-50 while also improving majority-class performance. Table 2 supports updating the visual-grammar model during continual learning, and the appendix examines several hyperparameters and backbones.
weaknesses: The central fairness argument does not establish its claimed geometric consequences. Proposition 1 derives an inverse-count optimum for normalized probabilities, but this does not imply that majority-class features are more compact. Features can have identical dot products with a centroid while differing substantially in orthogonal directions. Likewise, reducing the probability discrepancy in Proposition 2 does not establish reduced feature dispersion or improved classwise fairness.

Equation (4) has a consequential normalization ambiguity. The denominator is defined earlier over image features, without explicitly including the transition vector v, whereas Proposition 2 requires its probability to share the normalization. Under the literal feature-only denominator, increasing v·c makes the loss unbounded below. The stated objective therefore does not clearly support the proved optimum.

The cluster regularizer is inconsistent with the described optimization. Equation (8) optimizes segmentation parameters, but R_C depends only on centroids that are described as frozen or updated separately by momentum; Appendix 4 explicitly treats them as fixed during loss computation. Under this procedure, R_C supplies no gradient to the segmentation network. An additional differentiable update is needed to explain its reported contribution in Table 4. These unresolved objective and optimization issues outweigh the encouraging empirical results in my recommendation.

The claimed connection to knowledge distillation in Appendix 4 is unsupported for the actual loss. Equations (16)–(17) invoke a metric triangle inequality, but the contrastive objective is not shown to satisfy that property. Removing an additive constant through Big-O notation also does not establish that minimizing this objective preserves the proposed distillation constraint.

The ablations incompletely isolate the proposed mechanisms. The fairness loss changes both the contrastive weight and the transition-vector term, without a weight-matched vanilla-loss control. Removing visual grammar in Table 4 also changes the number of unknown clusters to one, confounding learned assignment with multiple-cluster modeling. Given the acknowledged foundations in parametric contrastive learning and Clusformer, these controls matter for establishing the contribution of the proposed adaptations.

Reproduction remains difficult despite the appendix's useful optimizer and memory settings. Important omissions include DBSCAN parameters, how old-class pixels are distinguished from unknown pixels before initialization, the visual-grammar pretraining procedure on ImageNet, and resolution of competing cluster assignments. The precise major/minor class partitions are also insufficiently specified, limiting independent verification of the fairness results.
